title: When the church does wrong
hook: the church has harmed people; honesty, repentance and justice are required

segments.voice: Yesterday, miracles: John calls them signs, and Augustine pointed at the vineyards. Your line was every day a miracle. What ordinary wonder did you catch and pass on? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

Some hard words about the church are inside the Bible itself. A letter of Peter puts it flatly: "For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God." Not out there, with the outsiders. At the house of God. That line matters, because churches have harmed people. Abuse, and abuse covered up. People shamed, driven out, told God was finished with them. Congregations that stood beside cruelty and called it order. Saying so out loud isn't an attack on faith. The Bible sets the pattern for it. Today: when the church does wrong.
screen: `JUDGMENT BEGINS AT THE HOUSE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: The Bible's word for what comes next is repent. And it gives three pictures here of what that looks like when a whole community has gone wrong. First, honesty that says we. In the book of Daniel, Daniel prays over the wrongs of his people. He doesn't point at them from a safe distance. He says, "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled." We. He stands inside the failure instead of beside it. Second, a turned life. To people coming out to be baptized, John the Baptist says: "Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance." Fruit you can see. In Luke, when people ask him what to do, his answers are concrete: share your coat, take no more than you're owed, don't bully anyone with your power. Repentance shows up in how you act on Monday. Third, repair. Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, and rich, meets Jesus, and in his own house he stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Not just sorry. Paid back, and more. Churches have tried to walk this road, some with public confessions, apologies, investigations and payments to survivors. Some have walked it well, some slowly, some not yet, and the people who were harmed are often the ones who can say how far it still has to go. In these texts, judgment begins at the house of God. So does repentance.

Here's the practice: pray for those hurt by churches. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people who have been harmed by a church: someone you know, someone whose story you've read, maybe yourself. You don't need details. Let them be real to you for a minute, without explaining their hurt away or rushing to defend anyone. If you pray, you can hold them before God, by name or in silence, and ask for truth, justice and healing for them. If you don't pray, simply hold them in mind with respect. The bell holds the time.
When the church does wrong. The Bible's answer is honest confession, a turned life and real repair, beginning at the house of God.
screen: `WHEN THE CHURCH DOES WRONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: repent. Today, if you owe someone an apology, make it plain, with no excuses attached, and ask what would help set it right. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Christians practice repentance through confession, private or in a liturgy, and churches of several traditions have made public confessions and apologies, opened independent investigations, and offered redress to people harmed by church leaders or institutions.

match.prompt: repentance in the Bible — tap the pairs.

myth: the Bible only criticizes outsiders, never God's own people
a letter of Peter says judgment must begin at the house of God.
Daniel confesses his people's wrongs as 'we', not 'they'
we have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled.
in these texts, repentance is just feeling sorry
John the Baptist asks for fruits meet for repentance, and Zacchaeus restores fourfold.

fork.setup: you're Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector, and Jesus has come to your house. people are muttering that he has gone to be the guest of a sinner. what do you do?
options: say nothing; the visit speaks for itself.
give half to the poor and pay back fourfold.
explain that everyone collects that way.
fork.reveal: Zacchaeus stands and promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone he wronged. Jesus says salvation has come to that house.

original.note: Greek: repentance — the word in "fruits meet for repentance" (Matthew 3:8).

trapdoor: what you thought: repent means feel bad about yourself.
what it means: in these texts repentance is honest confession, a changed life, and repair for the people who were wronged.
what a scholar hears: Daniel prays 'we have sinned' for his whole people, and Zacchaeus pays back fourfold. confession and restitution travel together.

notes: The harms named (abuse and cover-up, shaming and exclusion, churches standing beside cruelty) are general and name no church, event or date, per the claims rule. Keeper may want a more specific, carefully sourced example, or none.

'Churches have tried to walk this road, some with public confessions, apologies, investigations and payments to survivors' is a general statement not drawn from a cited text; confirm it is fair and not overstated.
Luke 3:10–14 summarized as 'share your coat, take no more than you're owed, don't bully anyone with your power'; confirm the paraphrase of 'do violence to no man'.
Original: μετάνοια in Matthew 3:8; the lesson avoids building on its etymology. Confirm.
Audit: fork setup now matches Luke 19:7 (the crowd murmurs that Jesus is the guest of a sinner), not 'muttering about what you've taken'.

Editor pass: cut the superlative "hardest words"; Matthew 3:8 is spoken to those coming to baptism (Matthew 3:7), not "crowds"; Zacchaeus no longer "grew rich at others' expense" or stands "at his own table" (Luke 19:2, 19:8 say only he was rich and stood).
